DANGER WILL, DANGER:
You are about to enter the ramblings of a lifetime King fan - beware all who enter. Much useless information follows.



"It's five minutes before nine...in Paris."

-----------------------CONNECTIONS-----------------------

When I began reading this story, roughly my sixtieth Stephen King novel or anthology, I had high expectations. I have long considered The Talisman my favorite SK book. It's central theme of a young boy maturing into manhood is a favorite. It also mirrored my life loosely as I had just lost my father when I read it at the age of twenty. Although not as monumental, like Jack, I was forced to grow up quickly and to make some tough decisions. Thank God the Multi-Verse wasn't dependent on my choices.Things around here might have been more like the end of 11/22/63.

Forty-five years have passed since I read that novel, Jack is now fifty-seven and I have ripened to retirement age. A lot has transpired since then, including a lifetime of reading about Annie Wilkes, Jack Torrance, Carrie White, Pennywise, and especially my favorite, Roland Deschain....THE GUNSLINGER!

" I do not kill with my gun; he who kills with his gun has forgotten the face of his father. I kill with my heart."

I haven't forgotten the face of my father, and I will take that memory and his love for me to the grave. This storyline just "connects" with me so strongly.

Secondly, knowing for months that this novel was close to release, and that even then it would be hard to justify its purchase financially (I'm living mostly on SS and own several hundred unread books) I forced myself to be patient and await my turn to get it electronically from Libby.
Thankfully, my wonderful wife gave me a HB copy on my 65th BD. It was literally the only recognition of my retirement and BD and yet felt like one of the greatest gifts I've ever received. My wife has been my biggest supporter while also being the most negatively impacted person from my obsession with books. Lisa, you are the best. Thank you for allowing me to visit other worlds all of these years.

Third thing. Shortly after beginning the book Jack begins to have these snippets of memory and we're given the phrase Le Salaire de la peur. Without reading further I begin researching this, find it's the title of a 1950 French novel, a 1953 movie adaptation, AND a reimagined film by William Friedkin named Sorcerer. I've long been a fan of that film and its' soundtrack by Tangerine Dream. Friedkin's combination of the story and their music is masterful and he creates an "atmosphere" overflowing with tension and dread.

Before I know what has happened my brain has led me down several webholes (shorter than writing rabbit holes, eh?) and I've sourced these remakes to the original French novel by Georges Arnaud, the '53 thriller directed by Henri-Georges Clouzot, then leaped to Friedkin's film and subsequently to a 2024 adaptation by Julien Leclercq, which....wait for it.... just happens to be available on Netflix. Well I have got to watch it, right? I believe I got through about a half hour of the film before I was summoned back to reality. I even went as far as adding the original novel to my TBR, adding comments to my own "add", and discussing fervently with my wife these various films, original books and adaptations, including my knowledge and appreciation of Tangerine Dreams music. All of that without remembering that the initial spark came from King's story. It was a full day later when I next picked up OWTT, read a reference to The Wages of Fear and realized my short term memory loss had done it to me again. Oddly, this can sometimes be entertaining and was this time..."connections."

I've recently written several reviews mentioning the overlap and the intertwining of narratives between various writers. Their work under pseudonyms, collaborative efforts, character homages, even their personal relationships have "connections." The sharing of story ideas at Astounding Science Fiction and John W. Campbell's influence on the works of multiple Sci-Fi masters was a recent discovery of mine. Lawrence Block's friendship with Donald E. Westlake another - Parker and Keller sure seem to be cut from the same mold. Add to all of that an entire life of reading these stories, watching the hundreds of television and cinematic versions and spin-offs, sharing these experiences with my friends, loved ones, and fellow readers and it has become impossible to overlook those "connections."

If not Stephen King, who else would we honor as the all-time great at creating such a vast library of stories, so many of which have connecting characters and storylines. Of intertwining an entire fantasy series with his other books, of weaving together The Territories with Mid-World, of blending Jack Sawyer with Roland, teasing us with his "twinners" theory. Who else could have pulled this off, including his fantastic collaboration choice of Peter Straub?

So, are the complaints about the length of this novel, the repetitiveness of his "twinner/echoes" theme, poor editing and what I perceived as some lazy work surrounding the Redheads legitimate? Yes, a resounding yes. I would probably rate it a four, possibly even slightly lower, but the experience I had while reading it, combined with all of the "connections" I've talked about, easily made this a five for me.

If you've "rambled" all the way to the end of this, thanks. Travelin' Jack would likely say "thankee sai."

P.S. Their is a scene where Jack watches one of the crazy birdberry dyed teenagers do a backflip and then scamper away. If you've ever seen The Road Warrior, you'll remember Wez, the Mohawked, leather bound, steel bolt wrist rocket toting maniac, standing on top of the bus at the refinery, evil incarnate, before backflipping off and "scampering away?

I think SK saw this film too.🤔
